problem: The premise and the physics are wrong. A lossy ground plane adds loss resistance, so the measured feed resistance goes up, not down. A small plane gives an imperfect image, which makes the structure behave more like the full dipole, again pushing the resistance up toward 73 Ω. The answer's line 'Both change the current distribution and lower the measured resistance' is the opposite of what both stated causes do.
fix: Change the question to: 'A student measures a quarter-wave monopole on a small metal box and finds its resistance quite different from 36.5 Ω. Suggest two causes.' Answer: (i) the ground plane is too small, so the image is imperfect and the antenna behaves partly like a full dipole, moving the resistance up toward 73 Ω; (ii) the plane is lossy, which adds loss resistance on top of the 36.5 Ω, so the measured value is higher; a third practical cause is common-mode current on the feed coax without a balun, which shifts the reading unpredictably.

problem: 'The feed current runs up one wire and back along the other, so both wires carry the same current I_in, in phase' reads as a contradiction: running up one wire and back along the other sounds like opposite directions, yet the sentence then says in phase. A student may conclude the two fields should cancel.
fix: 'The two wires are joined at both ends, so the feed current passes through both arms in series and both carry the same current I_in. The two arms radiate in phase, so their fields add.'

problem: 'Carry 73 Ω, 1.64 and 78° into any link budget' is misdirected: a link budget uses the gain (2.15 dBi) and, for coverage, the beamwidth. The 73 Ω is a matching quantity and does not appear in a link budget.
fix: 'Carry the gain 1.64 (2.15 dBi), and the 78° beamwidth if you are checking coverage, into any link budget (Chapter 2.8); the 73 Ω is what you match the feed line to.'
